sequence.title: Where does the extra money come from?
sequence.message: The bigger spending total is mostly paid for by a much bigger tax base: workers, companies, GST and super funds. Any remaining gap becomes deficit and debt.
sequence.visual_layout: Flow diagram: left side shows 2006 receipts; right side shows 2024-25 receipts. Use thick arrows for workers' income tax, company tax, GST, super, and a small debt-gap arrow.

facts.text: Total cash receipts rose from $236.7b in 2006-07 to $717.0b in 2024-25: about $480b more coming in each year
Individuals and other withholding tax rose from $115.8b to $338.3b: about $222.5b more
Company tax rose from $57.1b to $138.8b: about $81.7b more
GST receipts rose from $39.6b in 2006-07 to $90.3b in 2024-25: about $50.8b more
Superannuation fund taxes rose from $8.2b to $25.7b: about $17.5b more
When spending is still higher than receipts, the rest is financed by deficits and debt

sequence.title: Why can tax per person rise?
sequence.message: Governments can collect more per person without announcing a new tax: inflation, wage growth, bracket creep, bigger profits, service costs and debt repair all push…
sequence.visual_layout: Simple cause-and-effect board. Centre: 'more tax per person'. Around it: inflation, wages, bracket creep, more services, debt interest, budget repair. Add a final check: compare percentages, not just dollars.

facts.text: Inflation raises prices and nominal wages, so the same tax rates collect more dollars even before real living standards improve
Wage growth can push people into higher average tax rates in a progressive income tax system: the Parliamentary Budget Office calls this bracket creep
More people and more workers broaden the tax base, but per-person tax can still rise if incomes, prices and profits rise faster than population
Government can justify higher revenue by pointing to higher service costs: health, aged care, NDIS, defence, infrastructure and debt interest
Budget repair is another reason: governments may let bracket creep raise revenue, then later return some through tax cuts
The honest test is percentage burden, not just dollars: tax-to-income, tax-to-GDP, tax-to-budget and real per-person comparisons

sequence.title: Why is debt not being paid down?
sequence.message: More tax money does not automatically reduce debt. If spending promises, service costs and interest absorb the revenue, debt only falls when governments run sustained…
sequence.visual_layout: Leaky bucket visual: extra tax flows in at the top, then big holes drain to welfare, health, NDIS, states, defence, interest and new promises. Only leftover surplus flows to debt repayment.

facts.text: The key debt test is not whether revenue rises; it is whether revenue is bigger than spending and interest after every year’s promises
2025-26 expenses are estimated at $785.7b, while 2024-25 total receipts were about $717.0b: the annual budget is still very tight
Large fixed programs keep absorbing revenue: welfare $291b, health $125b, states GST support $101b, NDIS $52b and aged care $41b
Debt interest itself is now a major bill: debt management is about $28.4b in 2025-26
Surpluses in 2022-23 and 2023-24 helped, but they were not large enough to erase the accumulated debt stock
Politically, paying debt down means running sustained surpluses: higher taxes, lower services, slower benefit growth, or selling assets

sequence.title: The strongest case for taxing more
sequence.message: Supporters argue Australia should capture more value from public resources and use it for services, debt repair, or future generations.

sequence.title: The strongest case against taxing more
sequence.message: Opponents warn that sudden or poorly designed taxes can reduce investment, supply, jobs, or trust in policy rules.
sequence.visual_layout: Tax shock arrow leading to investor concern, then supply, jobs and policy-trust warning icons.

facts.text: The anti-tax case is strongest when focused on design risk, not blanket opposition
Bad timing or unstable rules can raise investment and supply concerns
The question is which risks are evidenced, exaggerated or manageable

sequence.title: The debate is really design
sequence.message: Once you get past slogans, the practical questions are rate, base, deductions, transition, price triggers, revenue use and transparency.
sequence.visual_layout: Checklist card titled 'Good tax design?' with seven ticks and a small warning icon for rushed design.

facts.text: Important design choices include rate, tax base, deductions and transition rules
A price trigger can target extra profits more narrowly than a broad permanent change
Public trust improves when revenue use and evidence are transparent

sequence.title: What each side leaves out
sequence.message: Industry often downplays public ownership and resource rent. Tax advocates can understate investment risk and design complexity.
sequence.visual_layout: Two-column card: 'industry may omit' and 'tax advocates may omit', with a fair-explanation bridge below.

facts.text: Industry messages may omit public ownership and rent-capture arguments
Tax-advocacy messages may omit investment, supply and design risks
A fair explanation should steelman both sides before concluding

sequence.title: The honest answer
sequence.message: More tax can be justified if it is evidence-based, stable, targeted at rents, transparent, and paired with a clear public benefit.
sequence.visual_layout: Balanced bridge between 'fair public return' and 'investment certainty', with a middle path labelled 'good design'.

facts.text: The honest question is not simply tax or no tax
Better question: what design gives Australians fair return without avoidable harm?
Clear public benefit and stable rules are central to legitimacy
